issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree requiring temporary continued occupation and later rehabilitation may become inexecutable when subsequent developments make its contemplated performance inconsistent with finalized planning requirements and overriding public needs.
material_facts: The decree allowed the shopkeepers to remain on the occupied sites temporarily and required their eventual relocation to a proposed shopping complex.
The shopping complex was never constructed, and both sides left the decree unexecuted for a prolonged period.
A later development plan reserved the occupied sites for a garden, and the structures were also found to fall within a highway control zone and to obstruct planned roads.
The decree did not determine ownership of the land or whether the structures complied with applicable regulatory requirements.
The later road and area-development measures were advanced as necessary for public access, safety, and convenience.
issues.conclusion: The compromise decree had become inexecutable in the circumstances, and the Court declined to interfere with that determination.
issues.legal_principle: Whether intervening developments make a decree inexecutable depends on the facts of the case. A court may take notice of subsequent events and altered circumstances where the relief has become inappropriate or cannot be given effect to, to shorten litigation, preserve the parties’ rights, and serve the ends of justice. The Court relied on M/s. Laxmi & Co. v. Dr. Anant R. Deshpande, Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University, and Arun Lal v. Union of India.

rule.if: execution_of_compromise_decree and decree_provides_temporary_occupation_pending_rehabilitation and (later_plan_conflicts_with_contemplated_use or structures_conflict_with_public_infrastructure_requirements) and prolonged_nonperformance

predicates.execution_of_compromise_decree: A party seeks to enforce a decree recording a compromise.
predicates.decree_provides_temporary_occupation_pen: The decree permits occupation to continue temporarily until the occupants are rehabilitated elsewhere.
predicates.later_plan_conflicts_with_contemplated_u: A finalized plan adopted after the decree reserves the occupied land for a use inconsistent with the decree’s contemplated construction or occupation.
predicates.structures_conflict_with_public_infrastr: The structures obstruct planned public roads or fall within a regulated area where the contemplated construction is not permitted.
predicates.prolonged_nonperformance: The parties leave the decree unperformed for a prolonged period.

issues.definition: When enforcement of a compromise decree providing temporary occupation pending rehabilitation conflicts with later finalized planning or public-infrastructure requirements after prolonged nonperformance, the decree may be treated as inexecutable.

issues.legal_issue: A local planning authority may issue a notice to remove structures to implement a development plan even when it does not own the land, and omission of a specific statutory section from the notice does not by itself invalidate it when the authority has the relevant statutory power.
material_facts: The land vested in the State, and the local authority was not a party to the earlier compromise decree.
The local authority was constituted as a planning authority and had statutory duties and powers concerning public streets, development plans, and unauthorized development.
The notice required removal of structures said to obstruct planned roads and conflict with the development plan and applicable restrictions.
The notice did not cite one statutory provision that empowered a planning authority to require discontinuance or removal in appropriate circumstances.
The occupants did not establish that their structures complied with the applicable statutory requirements.
issues.conclusion: The local authority was competent to issue the notice, its lack of ownership of the land was immaterial, and omission of the specific statutory section did not render the notice invalid; the challenge to the notice was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965, the Council is charged with municipal functions and has powers concerning obstructions and encroachments in public places and streets, including under Sections 49, 179, 180, and 189. Under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, a Council or Nagar Panchayat is a planning authority; Sections 42, 52, and 53 concern implementation of development plans and unauthorized development, while Section 56 authorizes action to discontinue or remove a use or development in the interest of proper planning. The Court held that the omission to mention Section 56 did not invalidate the notice in light of the authority’s statutory empowerment. The Bombay Highways Act, 1955, including Sections 3, 7, 9, and 73, provided for highway declarations, building and control lines, restrictions, and overriding effect in cases of inconsistency.

rule.if: challenge_to_removal_notice and issuing_authority_is_planning_authority and notice_seeks_to_implement_finalized_plan and (issuing_authority_does_not_own_land or notice_omits_specific_power_section) and occupants_do_not_show_statutory_compliance

predicates.challenge_to_removal_notice: An occupant brings a proceeding challenging a notice requiring removal or alteration of structures.
predicates.issuing_authority_is_planning_authority: The authority issuing the notice is legally constituted as a planning authority with statutory functions concerning development and public places.
predicates.notice_seeks_to_implement_finalized_plan: The notice seeks to address structures that obstruct or conflict with an adopted development plan.
predicates.issuing_authority_does_not_own_land: The authority issuing the notice is not the owner of the land on which the structures stand.
predicates.notice_omits_specific_power_section: The notice does not refer to a particular statutory provision that empowers the authority to direct discontinuance or removal.
predicates.occupants_do_not_show_statutory_complian: The occupants do not establish that their structures comply with the applicable regulatory requirements.

issues.definition: A removal notice seeking to implement a finalized plan is not invalid merely because the planning authority does not own the land or the notice omits a specific enabling section, where the occupants do not show statutory compliance.

issues.legal_issue: When removal of long-established business occupants is necessary to serve a substantial public interest, the authorities must make a sincere effort to provide a suitable alternative site and, if that effort fails, provide adequate compensation before taking further action to remove them.
material_facts: The occupants had continuously operated businesses on the sites for many years and relied on those businesses for their livelihood.
The Court accepted that removal was unavoidable to implement public development measures addressing road access, safety, security, and convenience.
The State reported that no vacant site was available in the immediate vicinity, despite the occupants proposing alternative sites.
Earlier compensation had been deposited, but the Court ordered a renewed assessment of relocation and compensation in light of the passage of time and the consequences of displacement.
The Court directed the State and relevant authorities to identify a suitable site and made compensation payable if a sincere effort did not identify a feasible alternative.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were dismissed subject to directions requiring an effort to identify a suitable alternative site and, if that effort proved unsuccessful, payment of adequate compensation; allotment of a site or deposit of compensation was a condition precedent to further action under the notice.
issues.legal_principle: Public welfare, including health, safety, law and order, and collective convenience, may take precedence over conflicting private interests. However, deprivation of property for public purpose under Article 300A requires public purpose and carries an entitlement to compensation; rehabilitation of displaced persons is also a relevant obligation. The Court relied on K.T. Plantation Private Limited v. State of Karnataka, Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, Tukaram Kana Joshi v. Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation, and K. Krishna Reddy v. Special Deputy Collector, including their treatment of public purpose, livelihood, rehabilitation, and the significance of timely compensation.

predicates.appeal_against_removal_for_public_purpos: Occupants appeal against action to remove them from a site for a public-purpose project or public-safety measure.
predicates.long_term_business_occupants_face_displa: People who have carried on business at the site for a prolonged period face displacement and loss of their established livelihood.
predicates.no_suitable_alternative_site_is_identifi: The responsible authorities make a sincere effort to find a suitable replacement site but identify none.
predicates.relocation_is_not_feasible: The authorities determine that the occupants cannot feasibly be accommodated at an alternative site.

issues.definition: When long-term business occupants face removal for a public purpose, the authorities must provide relocation or adequate compensation before removal if no suitable relocation is feasible.
